questions.question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

Everybody have contributed to the success of the fundraising campaign, demonstrating the collective effort and support for a worthy cause.

options.text: Everybody have contributed to the success
and support for a worthy cause.

questions.solution:
The erroneous part is **'Everybody have contributed to the success'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error in the given sentence is the use of "**have**" after "**everybody**." The correct form should be "**has**" because "**everybody**" is **a singular pronoun, **and it takes **a singular verb.**
 
• *Corrected sentence: **Everybody has contributed to the success **of the fundraising campaign, demonstrating the collective effort and support for a worthy cause. *
 
• "**Everybody**" is **an indefinite pronoun** that refers to every person, and it is treated as a singular noun. Therefore, it **takes a singular verb.**
 
• **Indefinite pronouns** such as*** 'someone, somebody, each, nobody, anyone, anybody, one no one, everyone, everybody, either, neither, etc.' ***always take** a singular verb.**
 
• In English, when **a singular subject is present**, the verb that follows it must also be in **the singular form**. Conversely, when dealing with **plural subjects, a plural verb is used.**
 
• *Example:*
 
 
• *Incorrect: **Everybody have **their own preferences when it comes to food.*
 
• *Correct: **Everybody has **their own preferences when it comes to food.*
 
 
 
• In the corrected example, "**has**" is used** to agree with the singular subject "everybody."**

questions.question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Instead of being (A)/ helpful he was (B)/ being hindrance (C)/ No Error (D)
questions.solution:
The erroneous part is** 'being hindrance'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• In the sentence, the phrase **"being hindrance"** is grammatically incorrect because it lacks an article before the noun** "hindrance."**
 
• **Articles** (like "**a**" or "**the**") are used **to specify or generalize a noun**. In this case, the noun "**hindrance**" refers to something that is causing **an obstruction or acting** as an obstacle.
 
• When using a **noun** like "**hindrance**," it usually requires **an** **article** before it to make the sentence grammatically accurate. The **corrected phrase** would be** "being a hindrance."** Here, "**a**" acts as** the indefinite article**, indicating that the person in question was acting as one among many possible hindrances.
 
• So, the revised sentence would be: *"Instead of being helpful, he was **being a hindrance.**"* This correction ensures grammatical accuracy by properly introducing the **noun** "**hindrance**" with the **necessary article. **

questions.question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

Supposing if it rains during the outdoor event, we should have a backup plan in place to ensure the success of the occasion.

options.text: we should have a backup plan in
place to ensure the success of the occasion

questions.solution:
The erroneous part is **'Supposing if it rains during'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error in the given sentence is the use of both** "supposing" and "if."** These terms convey a similar idea of assumption, and using them together is redundant. The correct form should be **"Supposing it rains" or "If it rains."**
 
• *Corrected sentence: **Supposing it rains during **the outdoor event, we should have a backup plan in place to ensure the success of the occasion.*
 
• **"Supposing" and "if"** both introduce a condition or assumption. Using them together is unnecessary and can create redundancy.
 
• *Example:*
 
 
• *Incorrect: **Supposing if **she forgets, we have a spare key.*
 
• *Correct: **Supposing** she forgets, we have a spare key. (or) If she forgets, we have a spare key.*
 
 
 
• In the corrected example, either** "Supposing" or "If" **is used to introduce the assumed condition, not both.

questions.question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Murph was among those luckiest woman who attained name and fame not by labour but by chance.

options.text: not by labour but by chance

questions.solution:
The erroneous part is **'those luckiest woman'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error in **the sentence** is in the **segment** which states** "those luckiest woman."** The correct phrasing should be** "those luckiest women."**
 
• Here's a more detailed breakdown:
 
 
• **"Woman"** is **a singular noun **referring to **one female individual.**
 
• When describing **a group of fortunate or lucky females**, the plural form "**women**" should be used. 
 
 
 
• Therefore, the corrected segment should read: *"Murph was among **those luckiest women** who attained name and fame not by labor but by chance."*
 
• The adjustment from "**woman**" to "**women**" ensures that **the plural form aligns **with the context of referring to **a group of lucky or fortunate females,** maintaining grammatical accuracy in the sentence.

questions.question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

Emirates Airlines is creating a lots of job opportunities in the US by placing orders for the Boeing flights.

options.text: creating a lots of job opportunities

questions.solution:
The erroneous part is** 'creating a lots of job opportunities****.'**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error in the sentence is in segment (**creating a lots of job opportunities**), where **"a lots of"** should be corrected to** "a lot of."**
 
• Here's the corrected sentence: *"Emirates airlines is **creating a lot of job opportunities** in the US by placing orders for Boeing flights."*
 
• The error lies in the incorrect usage of **"a lots of."** The correct phrase is **"a lot of," **which is used to indicate a large quantity or a considerable number of something. **"A lot of"** is used to describe a non-specific quantity, similar to "**many**" or "**numerous**."
 
• Here's an example to illustrate the correct usage:
 
 
• *Incorrect: "She has a lots of books on her shelf."*
 
• *Correct: "She has a lot of books on her shelf." *
 
 
 
• The correction clarifies that the sentence refers to a large number of job opportunities being created, using the appropriate and grammatically correct expression **"a lot of."**
 
• **correct sentence: "**Emirates Airlines is **creating a lot of job opportunities**__ in the US by placing orders for the Boeing flights."

questions.question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

He invited his three brother-in-laws to the family gathering.
questions.solution:
The erroneous part is** 'his three brother-in-laws'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error in the sentence is the use of **"brother-in-laws."** The correct plural form is **"brothers-in-law."**

 
 
• *Corrected sentence: "He invited **his three brothers-in-law **to the family gathering."*
 
 
 
• In compound nouns like **"brother-in-law,"** the primary noun ("**brother**") is made **plural** to indicate more than one, while the secondary part (**"in-law"**) remains unchanged. So, **"brothers-in-law" **is the correct plural form of "brother-in-law" when referring to multiple individuals. 
 
 
• *Example: "She consulted her two **sisters-in-law** about the family reunion."*
 
 
 
• In this corrected sentence,** "sister-in-law"** becomes **"sisters-in-law"** to indicate multiple sisters-in-law, following the rule where the primary noun ("**sister**") is pluralized, while the secondary part ("in-law") remains the same.
 
• Similarly, **"brothers-in-law"** should be used to indicate multiple **brothers-in-law** in the sentence provided.

questions.question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

Knowing the opponent was enough cunning to anticipate conventional strategies, the chess player devised a clever and unexpected move to gain an advantage in the game.

options.text: enough cunning to anticipate conventional strategies
the chess player devised a clever
and unexpected move to gain an advantage in the game

questions.solution:
The erroneous part is **'​enough cunning to anticipate conventional strategies'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error in the given sentence is the placement of **"enough" before "cunning." **The correct form is** "cunning enough."**
 
• *Corrected sentence: Knowing the opponent was **cunning enough to anticipate conventional strategies**, the chess player devised a clever and unexpected move to gain an advantage in the game.*
 
• When describing a degree or extent, the **adjective "enough"** typically follows** the adjective it modifies. **In this case, "**cunning**" is** the adjective** describing the opponent, and "**enough**" should come after it.
 
• *Example:*
 
 
• *Incorrect: She was **enough intelligent **to solve the complex puzzle.*
 
• *Correct: She was **intelligent enough** to solve the complex puzzle. *
 
 
 
• In the corrected example,** "intelligent enough" **is the correct placement of "**enough**" after the** adjective "intelligent" **to express the degree of intelligence.

questions.question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

She is both intelligent as well as creative, excelling in academic pursuits and artistic endeavors.

options.text: She is both intelligent as well as creative,

questions.solution:
The erroneous part is** 'as well as creative'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The error in the given sentence is the use of both "**both**" and "**as well as**" together, which creates redundancy. Either "**both**" or "**as well as**" is sufficient **to convey the idea of inclusion.**
 
• **'Both'** and **'and'** are **correlative conjunctions** and hence, they must be used together.
 
• *Corrected sentence: She is **both intelligent and creative,** excelling in academic pursuits and artistic endeavors.*
 
• "**Both**" is used to indicate the combination of two elements, and** "as well as" **also serves the same purpose. Using both** together is redundant.**
 
• *Example:*
 
 
• *Incorrect: He is **both a talented musician as well as** a skilled songwriter.*
 
• *Correct: He is** both a talented musician and **a skilled songwriter.*
 
 
 
• In the corrected example, "**both**" is used alone **to effectively convey the combination of talents without redundancy.**
